neighbours.label: how a celestial body is oriented toward its star: axial tilt, seasons, tidal locking (fires on the clause describing the orientation)
fire: Uranus is tipped on its side, so each pole gets decades of constant daylight.
On Earth, June is warm in the north because that half leans toward the sun.
Since Jupiter barely tilts, the giant planet has almost no seasons at all.
Many exoplanets near red dwarfs keep the same face turned to their star.
In winter the southern hemisphere points away from the sun and days grow short.
Saturn's tilt of about 27 degrees gives it long seasons lasting seven years.
Mercury rotates three times for every two orbits, so its days are very long.
Because the axis is inclined, sunlight hits the ground at a lower angle in December.
quiet: Uranus is an ice giant made mostly of water, ammonia and methane.
On Earth, June is a popular month for weddings and graduations.
Jupiter is so large that more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it.
Many exoplanets near red dwarfs were found by the TESS space telescope.
In winter the southern ocean is rough and many ships stay in port.
Saturn's rings are made of ice and rock ranging from dust to boulders.
Mercury has a huge iron core that fills most of its interior.
Because the telescope is new, astronomers are still calibrating its camera.

notes: Top examples all describe hemispheres leaning toward the sun, seasons from tilt, tidal locking, elongation angle. Probe: other planetary facts (moons, composition) stay low.
